title: Plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) is a biomarker for central nervous system involvement in infantile-onset Pompe disease

Summary Background Pompe disease (PD), caused by acid α-glucosidase (GAA) deficiency, leads to glycogen accumulation in various tissues including the central nervous system. While enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) is lifesaving, it does not cross the blood–brain barrier. CNS manifestations including sensorineural hearing loss, dysarthria, and cognitive delay—persist despite ERT. Hence, CNS-specific biomarkers are needed to identify at-risk patients and guide monitoring and treatment. This clinical, retrospective study evaluated the utility of plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) as a potential biomarker of CNS involvement in infantile-onset Pompe disease (IOPD) compared to plasma neurofilament light chain (NfL). Methods Plasma GFAP and NfL levels were measured longitudinally in 37 patients with PD (180 samples, ages 0.1–21 years) and 54 age- and sex-matched controls. Patients were grouped as (1) IOPD with severe neurologic involvement (n = 7), (2) IOPD with attenuated neurologic involvement (n = 13), and (3) late-onset PD without neurologic involvement (LOPD; n = 17). Neurologic status was determined via clinical examination and/or brain MRI white matter grading via Modified Fazekas Scores (MFS). Findings GFAP levels were highest in IOPD patients with severe neurologic involvement. Patients with IOPD in the attenuated neurologic involvement group had, on average, lower plasma GFAP concentrations than those with severe neurologic involvement but greater GFAP levels than patients with LOPD, which resembled controls. GFAP outperformed NfL in differentiating patients with IOPD from controls (AUC = 0.886 vs 0.705) and identifying severe from attenuated neurologic involvement group (AUC = 0.801 vs 0.745). NfL showed high variability between controls and PD subgroups. Interpretation Plasma GFAP levels reliably reflect CNS disease burden in IOPD and outperform NfL in diagnostic performance. GFAP may be a useful biomarker for detecting and monitoring CNS involvement in PD. Funding Funding was provided in part by 10.13039/100004339 Sanofi (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA). Clinical phenotypes of PD range from the severe infantile-onset form (IOPD), characterised clinically by cardiomyopathy and hypotonia within the first days to weeks of life, to the late-onset form (LOPD), which involves a more slowly progressive myopathy. The advent of enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with recombinant human GAA (rhGAA) has allowed for prolonged survival, improved cardiomyopathy, and achievement of motor milestones for patients with PD. However, ERT is unable to cross the blood–brain barrier (BBB) and as patients with IOPD live longer, clinical signs of neurologic involvement have been revealed. The phenotypic spectrum of central nervous system (CNS) involvement in IOPD spans from mild (attenuated) manifestations, like sensorineural hearing loss, and dysarthria, to the more severe manifestations, including seizures and encephalopathy. White matter hyperintensities (WMHI) on brain imaging have been shown to be progressive, more severe in patients with IOPD, and associated with cognitive deficits. As novel therapies capable of crossing the BBB are developed, identification of blood-based biomarkers that reliably detect and quantify CNS involvement are imperative for guiding and monitoring treatment. Prior studies have evaluated the utility of neurofilament light chain (NfL), a marker of axonal damage, as a prospective biomarker of CNS involvement in IOPD. However, NfL is expressed by neurons in both the central and peripheral nervous system, and therefore, is not a specific indicator of CNS pathology. To date, no study has evaluated plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) as a potential biomarker of CNS involvement in IOPD. Added value of this study We demonstrated that plasma GFAP outperformed NfL in differentiating IOPD patients with severe neurologic involvement from those with attenuated neurologic involvement. GFAP demonstrated greater discriminatory performance between healthy controls and patients with IOPD who had attenuated or severe neurologic involvement. Plasma GFAP levels positively correlated with WMHI on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) such that patients with greater WMHI also had the highest plasma GFAP concentrations. Implications of all the available evidence Our study shows that plasma GFAP is a sensitive and specific biomarker of neurological changes in IOPD and may detect CNS involvement more reliably than NfL. Our work highlights the potential of plasma GFAP as tool to detect and monitor CNS involvement in patients with IOPD, especially when taken in conjunction with other outcomes, such as WMHI patterns, clinical neurologic exam findings, and biomarkers, such as NfL, that are being used to characterise the natural history of CNS involvement in IOPD. Introduction Pompe disease (PD), also known as glycogen storage disease type II, is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA). Deficiency of GAA leads to the accumulation of glycogen in various tissues, notably in cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle, and in the central nervous system (CNS). 1 Clinically, PD presents as a spectrum, ranging from the severe infantile-onset form (IOPD), characterised by cardiomyopathy and profound muscle weakness within the first few days to weeks of life, to the late-onset form (LOPD), which predominantly involves skeletal muscle without cardiac involvement in the first year of life. 2 , 3 Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with recombinant human GAA (rhGAA) has significantly improved survival and quality of life in patients with PD. 4 , 5 Unfortunately, current ERT regimens approved for PD—including next generation ERTs—do not cross the blood–brain barrier (BBB). 6 As patients with IOPD live longer with ERT, a new natural history with neurologic involvement has emerged. Recent studies have demonstrated involvement of both the CNS and peripheral nervous system (PNS) in IOPD. 7 , 8 CNS manifestations of IOPD include sensorineural hearing loss, dysarthria, white matter hyperintensities (WMHI) on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), neuropsychological abnormalities, and in severe cases, seizures and encephalopathy. 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 To address CNS involvement in IOPD, therapies capable of crossing the BBB are in development, including modified enzyme replacement therapies that incorporate BBB-crossing tags (fusion proteins enabling receptor-mediated transport) and gene therapy approaches. 15 , 16 Given that various therapies targeting the CNS are on the horizon, there is a pressing need for blood-based biomarkers that can detect and monitor CNS involvement. Neurofilament light chain (NfL), a well-established marker for neuroaxonal injury, has demonstrated its utility across a range of neurologic disorders such as spinal muscular atrophy, 17 metachromatic leukodystrophy, 18 X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, multiple sclerosis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome. 19 Recent evidence has demonstrated the potential utility of plasma NfL in IOPD. 13 , 20 Despite these encouraging results, NfL levels can reflect both CNS and PNS axonal injury and thus reduces its specificity for CNS involvement in IOPD. Furthermore, NfL levels predominantly reflect neuroaxonal degeneration, including pathology in motor neurons, yet do not reflect astrocytic or other glial pathology often associated with white matter disease which has been noted in IOPD. 10 , 11 , 21 Collectively, this limits NfL's ability to fully represent the spectrum of CNS involvement in IOPD, particularly in cases with predominant gliosis and white matter changes. In contrast, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) is an intermediate filament protein predominantly expressed by astrocytes in the CNS, with minimal expression in the PNS, 22 and is released into the bloodstream following astrocyte activation, either due to BBB disruption or via glymphatic clearance. Additionally, GFAP has a shorter half-life in circulation compared to NfL, 22 , 23 , 24 suggesting it could be a more sensitive indicator of CNS involvement in IOPD. This study investigates the utility of plasma GFAP as a biomarker for detecting and monitoring CNS involvement in PD. We evaluated plasma GFAP levels across defined PD cohorts—those with severe, attenuated, or no neurologic involvement—to identify differences between groups and correlations with brain MRI findings. In addition, we compared plasma GFAP and NfL levels to evaluate their specificity and sensitivity for CNS pathology. Methods Ethics This study was conducted under protocols approved by the Duke University Institutional Review Board (IRB), including Pro00010830, Pro00072329, and Pro00007612 for the use of PD patient samples and clinical data, and Pro000072329 for control samples obtained from remnant blood referred for clinical testing at the Duke University Health System Biochemical Genetics Laboratory. Longitudinal brain MRI scans were conducted under IRB-approved protocols with appropriate oversight. Written informed consent for participation in research was obtained from all participants or their legally authorised representatives. In the case of paediatric participants, informed consent was obtained from parents or legal guardians in accordance with institutional and national guidelines. Inclusion criteria Eligibility criteria included a confirmed diagnosis of PD, availability of at least two plasma samples in the biorepository collected from the earliest collection date to May 2024, and either at least one brain MRI and/or a clinical neurologic assessment time-matched with blood collection, which was used to determine cohort assignment based on the degree of neurologic involvement ( Fig. 1 ). Specifically, patients with IOPD were defined as those presenting within the first year of life with cardiomyopathy, whereas patients with LOPD were defined as those without cardiomyopathy in the first year of life, consistent with the definition adopted by Slonim et al., 2000; Kishnani et al., 2006. 2 , 3 Neurologic phenotype classification Neurologic involvement in IOPD was classified retrospectively at database lock based on each patient's most recent MRI findings and clinical exams. Severe neurologic involvement was defined by diffuse, high-grade WMHI (Modified Fazekas Score ≥20/45) and/or severe neurologic features such as seizures or encephalopathy. Attenuated neurologic involvement was defined by lower WMHI burden (Modified Fazekas Score <20), with only mild neurologic features such as sensorineural hearing loss, dysarthria, or hypo/hyperreflexia. Importantly, no patient in the attenuated neurologic involvement group progressed to the severe neurologic phenotype during the assessment period. Please refer to Fig. 1 for detailed description and cohort assignment. Blood sample collection and assays Longitudinal plasma samples were obtained from all participants during standard of care clinical visits. As sampling was performed during routine follow-up rather than predefined intervals, the frequency and timing of samples per patient varied. In all cases, including those who subsequently developed severe neurologic involvement, sampling began prior to the onset of neurologic signs and symptoms. Similarly, age- and sex-matched plasma samples from non-PD individuals without a documented history of traumatic brain injury, neurologic or neuromuscular disorders, or neurodevelopmental concerns were included as controls (n = 54). These samples were derived from remnant blood referred to the Duke University Health System Biochemical Genetics Laboratory for testing (IRB# Pro000072329) and were collected for non-neurologic evaluations such as metabolic, haematologic, dermatologic, or infectious workups. Clinical data associated with each control sample were reviewed to confirm the absence of neurologic symptoms or diagnoses at the time of specimen collection. Levels of GFAP and NfL were quantified in plasma samples using Simoa® Neurology 2-Plex B Kits at the Molecular Genomics Core at Duke Molecular Physiology Institute. Sample analysis was performed blinded and in duplicate to ensure accuracy and consistency. Values were expressed in picogramme per millilitre (pg/ml). Brain neuroimaging Longitudinal brain MRI scans were performed on patients aged 5 years and older to minimise sedation-related risks and to capture early white matter changes, as supported by our previous findings. 25 Scans were acquired using Siemens Prisma (Munich, Germany) 3.0 T MRI Scanner (MAGNETOM Trio) with MR XA30A software and an 8-channel head coil. Non-contrast T1, T2 and T2-fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences were obtained and assessed for WMHI using the Modified Fazekas Score (MFS) by a neuroradiologist (M.M.) with expertise in PD, who was blinded to the clinical status and neurologic findings of each patient. The MFS, which evaluates 9 brain areas across superficial and deep white matter regions, similar to the original Fazekas Score published by our group, 26 provides more precise quantification and allows the inclusion of additional brain regions as well as qualitative assessment of cortical atrophy (included as addendum ‘V’ to the total sum score). A full description of the MFS, its scoring regions, evolution, and rationale for modification is available in our recently published long-term outcomes study in IOPD. 27 Further details are also provided in Supplementary Table S2 . Statistics Statistical analyses were independently conducted and reviewed by two individuals with expertise in biostatistics to ensure accuracy. Demographic and clinical data were compared between the defined patient groups: no, attenuated, or severe neurologic involvement. Continuous variables were compared using a Kruskal–Wallis test and categorical variables were compared using a chi squared test. All plasma GFAP and NfL measurements from the PD cohort and controls were treated as independent data points. Plasma GFAP and NfL measurements taken within the same calendar year were averaged in order to reduce bias towards participants with greater number of measurements. The median concentrations of both GFAP and NfL were compared between different groups of PD and controls using the Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's post-hoc analysis. A Bonferroni correction was applied for multiple comparisons. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were constructed using the observed biomarker values to evaluate the ability of GFAP and NfL concentrations to: (1) discriminate patients with IOPD from controls and (2) identify patients with IOPD at risk for severe neurologic phenotypes. These analyses were exploratory and conducted on the full dataset without the separate validation cohort. The performances of the ROC curves were evaluated by calculating the area under the curve (AUC) and comparing the AUCs with the DeLong test. Spearman correlation analysis was used to study the relationship between biomarker concentrations and MFS in patients with IOPD patients for whom blood samples were collected concurrently with brain MRIs, which was defined as within three months of sample collection. In participants for which plasma GFAP and NfL taken within the same calendar year were averaged, the average biomarker concentration and MRI data from the corresponding year were used. The r-value and p-value are displayed alongside scatterplots. All error bars represent the standard error. p-values less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism version 10.0.0 for Windows (GraphPad Software, Boston, MA, USA). Role of funders The funders of this study had no role in study design, data collection, data analyses, interpretation, or writing of the report. Results The study involved 37 patients with PD (20 IOPD and 17 LOPD), classified into three groups. The severe neurologic involvement group (n = 7, all IOPD) included both CRIM-negative (n = 2) and CRIM-positive (n = 5) patients, diagnosed at a median age of 0.2 years (range: birth–0.5 years), with ERT (standard dose of rhGAA, i.e. 20 mg/kg every other week) initiation at a median age of 0.2 years (range: 0.1–0.6 years) and plasma samples collected between ages 0.12 and 12.47 years. The attenuated neurologic involvement group (n = 13) consisted of 12 CRIM-positive and 1 CRIM-negative patients with IOPD, diagnosed at a median age of 0.2 years (range: birth–1.1 years), ERT initiation at a median age of 0.2 years (range: birth–1.1 years), and samples collected between ages 0.15 and 21.20 years. Similarly, the no neurologic involvement group (n = 17, all paediatric patients with LOPD) had a median age at diagnosis of 1.1 years (range: 0–11.1 years), 15 out of 17 patients were on ERT with initiation at a median age of 3.0 years (range: 0.1–11.7 years) and had plasma samples collected between ages 0.37 and 19.49 years. At the time of database lock, the median age of the cohort was 12.4 years (range: 0.12–21.20 years). The distribution of sample ages differed between groups: for example, 50% of samples from patients with IOPD with severe neurologic involvement were obtained by age 6, compared to age 10 in the attenuated neurologic involvement group, reflecting the more rapid disease course in the severe neurologic involvement subgroup. The seven patients with IOPD with severe neurologic involvement all had high WMH burden (median most recent MFS = 24) and several experienced seizures or encephalopathy. In contrast, the twelve patients with attenuated neurologic involvement had lower WMHI scores (median most recent MFS = 4.5) and no seizures, though mild neurologic findings such as sensorineural hearing loss, dysarthria, hypo/hyperreflexia were common. Additional clinical and demographic details are provided in Table 1 . GAA variant and GAA enzyme activity information is provided in Supplementary Table S1 . Plasma GFAP and NfL levels differ across clinical subgroups of IOPD Plasma GFAP levels were consistently elevated across all longitudinal samples in both IOPD subgroups compared with controls (p < 0.001; Fig. 2 A). The highest levels were observed in patients with severe neurologic involvement (median: 2094 pg/mL, range: 256.9–8157), followed by those with attenuated neurologic involvement (median: 688.6 pg/mL, range: 31.2–3969). Plasma GFAP levels of the LOPD with no neurologic involvement group (median: 89.6 pg/mL, range: 22.7–332.6) resembled that of controls (median: 109.1 pg/mL, range: 22.7–701.7). Plasma GFAP concentrations in both IOPD subgroups were higher than those in LOPD with no neurologic involvement and controls, although the pattern differed by subgroup and age ( Fig. 3 A). The IOPD subgroup with severe neurologic involvement showed markedly elevated GFAP from infancy onward, with 8 of the 10 samples in the first year exceeding concentrations above 1000 pg/mL, a threshold roughly 5 times higher than the maximum observed in controls of age <1 yrs (n = 5), though numbers were too small for statistical comparison. In the IOPD group with attenuated neurologic involvement, GFAP levels overlapped with those of controls and the LOPD group during early childhood but gradually increased over time. From approximately 8–10 years of age onward, GFAP levels in the IOPD with attenuated neurologic involvement all began to exceed those observed in controls and patients with LOPD. In contrast, GFAP levels and trends in the LOPD group were comparable to those in controls throughout, with minimal variability and only rare outliers. Group-level comparisons confirmed that the IOPD with severe neurologic involvement had significantly higher GFAP levels compared to the attenuated neurologic subgroup (p < 0.001; Fig. 2 A). In contrast, plasma NfL levels were not consistently elevated in the IOPD groups. Median NfL concentrations were 9.4 pg/mL (range: 1.8–34.4) in the severe neurologic involvement subgroup, 3.9 pg/mL (range: 0.5–16.1) in the attenuated neurologic involvement subgroup, 2.7 pg/mL (range: 0.3–28.9) in LOPD and 7 pg/mL (range: 2.6–82.9) in controls. Interestingly, several controls exhibited NfL concentrations within or above the range observed in patients with IOPD with attenuated and severe neurologic involvement, resulting in substantial overlap across groups and highlighting the high inter-individual variability observed across all cohorts and ages ( Figs. 2 B and 3 B). This variability partly reflects known physiological age effects on NfL concentrations, with higher values observed in infants compared to older children and adolescents. In fact, controls demonstrated significantly higher NfL concentrations compared to both LOPD and IOPD with attenuated neurologic involvement groups (p < 0.001, Fig. 2 B). There was no significant difference in NfL concentration between controls and the IOPD severe neurologic involvement. Additionally, no clear difference in GFAP or NfL was observed based solely on CRIM status of these participants. Comparison of the ability of plasma GFAP and NfL for classifying IOPD and its neurologic subgroups ROC analysis revealed that plasma GFAP had a higher discriminatory performance than plasma NfL in differentiating IOPD from controls (AUC = 0.886 vs 0.705; p < 0.001; Fig. 4 A and B) and in distinguishing severe from attenuated neurologic involvement within the IOPD group (AUC = 0.801 vs 0.7451; Fig. 4 C and D). Although plasma GFAP levels showed a trend toward improved classification of disease severity, the difference compared with plasma NfL levels did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.55). Correlation of plasma GFAP and NfL levels with white matter hyperintensities in brain MRI Plasma GFAP levels showed a stronger correlation with WMHI scores (r = 0.855, p < 0.001; Fig. 5 A) compared with plasma NfL levels (r = 0.711, p < 0.001; Fig. 5 B). Specifically, plasma GFAP levels tended to increase with higher WMHI scores such that patients with the highest WMHI also had some of the highest plasma GFAP concentrations. However, considerable variability, in both GFAP and NfL plasma levels, was observed in patients with moderate WMHI (MFS scores between 17 and 19). Discussion In patients with IOPD, there is a growing understanding of the pathological role of glycogen accumulation in the CNS. Although ERT has markedly improved survival, enabling many individuals with IOPD to reach adulthood, its inability to cross the BBB has resulted in a new natural history with emerging CNS manifestations. 8 , 10 , 11 , 13 , 20 , 28 Although human neuropathological data are limited, early autopsy studies in patients with IOPD aged 2.5 months to 2 years have revealed glycogen accumulation in neurons, glial cells, and cerebral vasculature across multiple brain regions, including the cortex, brainstem, and cerebellum. 7 , 8 , 29 , 30 , 31 These findings suggest diffuse CNS involvement, but many aspects of IOPD-related CNS pathology remain poorly understood. Currently, there are no reliable clinical or radiological predictors of which patients will go on to develop severe neurologic involvement, making it challenging to identify those at highest risk. As therapeutic innovations targeting CNS delivery across the BBB are emerging, early identification of at-risk individuals will also be critical for stratifying patients in clinical trials. Hence, blood-based CNS-specific biomarkers are needed to identify and track neurologic progression in long-term survivors with IOPD. NfL, a marker of neuroaxonal injury, has shown utility in various neurodegenerative and neurometabolic conditions affecting the CNS and PNS. Recent studies have explored the utility of plasma NfL in IOPD, with varying conclusions. In a cohort of 11 early treated patients with IOPD aged 0.06 years (approximately 22 days) to 21.2 years, Mackenbach et al. reported a gradual increase in serum NfL levels over time, with levels significantly elevated compared to controls, and interestingly, higher in CRIM-positive (n = 12) compared to CRIM negative patients (n = 4). These findings support the potential of NfL as a biomarker of CNS involvement in IOPD. 13 Hsu et al. also demonstrated a positive correlation between plasma NfL levels and MRI severity scores in 18 patients with IOPD aged 4–19 years. 20 However, their study was limited by the lack of serial NfL measurements, incomplete neuroimaging in younger patients, and the absence of biomarker-negative individuals without CNS abnormalities for comparison. Our study builds on this prior work by evaluating NfL, as previously published, and GFAP. In addition, we stratified by detailed neurologic and radiological phenotypes. We included patients with IOPD (both CRIM-positive and CRIM-negative), patients with LOPD, and unaffected controls without a history of CNS disease, trauma, or neurodevelopmental concerns. Although elevated NfL levels were observed only in the IOPD subgroup with severe neurologic involvement, we observed substantial inter-individual variability, including some elevated values in controls and patients with LOPD without CNS involvement and normal brain MRIs. One possible explanation for this overlap is the known involvement of lower motor neurons, including anterior horn cells, in both patients with IOPD and LOPD without overt CNS manifestations. 32 , 33 Since NfL reflects axonal damage from both central and peripheral sources, elevations in NfL may partly reflect lower motor neuron or peripheral nerve involvement rather than CNS pathology alone. This lack of tissue specificity likely contributed to the trends we observed with group-level differences and underscores NfL's limited sensitivity for detecting early or subclinical CNS involvement in IOPD. Furthermore, this variability may also be influenced by factors such as age, genotype and disease burden. Another possible contributor is that while none of the controls had documented CNS disease at the time of sampling, it is possible that some had early or subclinical pathology that contributed to elevated NfL values. In contrast, GFAP is a CNS-specific intermediate filament protein predominantly expressed by astrocytes, and its elevation in circulation reflects astrocyte activation or injury in response to various CNS insults, including neuroinflammation, trauma, ischaemia or chronic neurodegenerative processes. It is an established biomarker of astrogliosis in neurometabolic disorders such as metachromatic leukodystrophy, 18 as well as in conditions like traumatic brain injury, 34 stroke, 35 and neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease. 36 , 37 Given its CNS specificity, shorter half-life, and sensitivity to subtle glial changes, GFAP offers a dynamic and targeted biomarker for CNS pathology in IOPD—capturing astroglial responses that are not reflected by neuroaxonal markers like NfL. Astrocytes are vital to CNS homoeostasis, playing essential roles in neurotransmitter recycling, synaptic integrity, and metabolic support of neurons. 38 Their activation can have widespread consequences on neuronal health and signalling. Autopsy studies of IOPD have revealed marked astrocyte activation, suggesting a key role of astroglial involvement in CNS pathology. 11 , 16 To provide a histopathological context, in the GAA 6neo/6neo knock-out mouse model of PD, we observed increased GFAP immunostaining in the cerebral cortex (grey matter), brainstem and cerebellar white matter ( Supplementary Figure S1 ), supporting the concept that astroglial activation contributes to the elevated plasma GFAP seen in IOPD and highlighting the need for further confirmation in human autopsy studies. Because our cohort was small and the number of longitudinal plasma samples per participant was highly variable, we were unable to perform reliable age-stratified regression modelling. Therefore, group differences were summarised using median values. Despite this limitation, our analysis showed markedly elevated plasma GFAP levels in both subgroups of neurologic involvement in patients with IOPD compared to patients with LOPD and controls. Levels were highest in those with severe neurologic involvement. Most patients with attenuated neurologic involvement also exhibited elevated GFAP concentrations—often preceding the appearance of white matter changes on MRI. However, this should be confirmed with future studies with a larger longitudinal cohort. This is particularly relevant for individuals who may appear clinically stable but exhibit rising GFAP levels. In our experience, several such patients (S1, S2, and S3, corresponding to IDs 5, 2, and 4 in our prior seizure cohort study) demonstrated persistently elevated GFAP levels from early childhood, preceding both seizure onset and progressive MRI findings. 12 These observations underscore the importance of early identification and close neurological monitoring, even in patients with initial mild neurologic involvement. Importantly, in our cohort, patients classified to attenuated neurologic group remained so throughout their observation period; none progressed to the severe neurologic phenotype within the timeframe of this study, though longer follow-up will be important to assess whether some eventually do so. Similarly, in patients with LOPD, the GFAP levels remained within control range, reinforcing its specificity for CNS pathology in IOPD. The ROC analyses and higher AUC values further supported GFAP's potential as a discriminatory indicator compared to NfL, for both distinguishing IOPD from controls and identifying severe CNS involvement within IOPD group. Interestingly, elevated GFAP levels were observed in some patients with only mild WMHI on MRI, suggesting the possibility of subclinical CNS injury not yet visible on MRI, or astroglial activation in regions not captured by white matter–focused imaging, such as cortex and other grey matter structures. The Modified Fazekas Score (MFS) used in our study quantifies WMHI but does not evaluate grey matter regions, where astrocytes are also abundant. GFAP may thus reflect a broader spectrum of astrocytic activation, including in regions beyond the scope of standard neuroimaging and the currently used visual grading systems such as the original Fazekas Score (FS), our Modified Fazekas Score (MFS), and region-based qualitative approaches described by Ebbink et al. and subsequent modification of this method described by Dorpel et al. 10 , 14 , 26 This hypothesis is also supported by findings in GAA 6neo/6neo knockout (KO) mice, which showed increased GFAP expression in the cerebral cortex, brainstem, and cerebellar white matter. Given that the murine brain is predominantly composed of grey matter, and that GFAP increases were especially notable in the cortex, these findings underscore the sensitivity of astroglial responses even in regions lacking overt structural injury. Moreover, GFAP may be sensitive to diffuse astroglial pathology, BBB dysfunction, and glymphatic disruption—features that precede structural damage visible on MRI. Future studies investigating the use of alternative advanced quantitative approaches (e.g., automated lesion segmentation tools for FLAIR images such as the Lesion Segmentation Toolbox with the Lesion Prediction Algorithm) could be helpful. Employing such methods in future studies may better characterise the extent of WMHI and could even reveal subtle changes correlating with biomarker levels. Our findings also highlight the stronger correlation of GFAP with WMHI scores (r = 0.855) compared to NfL (r = 0.711). Taken together with the results of our ROC analysis, these findings support the use of plasma GFAP as a more specific biomarker of CNS involvement in IOPD, with potential utility for early detection, individualised monitoring, and future clinical trial endpoints. However, there was wide variability in plasma GFAP levels (1183.1–3802.3 pg/mL) of patients in the attenuated neurologic involvement group with MFS scores of 17–19, which demonstrates the importance of further research to identify risk factors and sensitive monitoring strategies in this subsect of patients with IOPD with WMHI scores that closely resemble those associated with the severe neurologic involvement phenotype. Additionally, further study is warranted to determine the relationship between plasma GFAP and additional clinical outcomes such as cognition and processing speed. Several studies have utilised the same research-grade assay to evaluate the utility of NfL in neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. 39 Notably, the NfL concentrations reported in those cohorts were much higher than those observed in our patients with IOPD. This contrast underscores an important distinction: in classical neurodegenerative disorders, the burden of axonal injury is substantial and widespread, leading to consistently elevated NfL levels. In contrast, IOPD is a metabolic disorder with CNS involvement that extends beyond motor neurons. This likely accounts for the less consistent NfL elevations observed in our cohort. It is important to note that while we highlight NfL's lack of specificity (due to PNS contributions) as a limitation for detecting CNS involvement, this does not diminish the relevance of PNS pathology in IOPD. Indeed, elevated NfL in our patients may partly reflect peripheral nerve or motor neuron involvement. However, in the context of identifying a biomarker more specific to CNS pathology, GFAP appears to provide better localisation to astroglial activation within the brain. GFAP showed stronger associations with WMHI burden and better group separation than NfL, supporting its specificity as a marker of astroglial activation within the brain. Considered together, the two biomarkers provide complimentary insights− NfL capturing axonal degeneration and GFAP reflecting astroglial response, thereby offering a more integrated view of neurologic involvement in IOPD. Data on the relationship between plasma NfL and GFAP in our cohort is provided in Supplementary Figure S2 . Investigation into the utility of a composite measure, taking into account NfL and GFAP, is warranted. When paired with brain MRI, this combined approach could enable earlier recognition of subclinical CNS injury and allow early CNS targeted treatment interventions. Current clinical monitoring of IOPD includes routine measurement of muscle-based biomarkers such as creatine kinase (CK), as well as urinary glucose tetrasaccharide and muscle imaging. In our cohort, correlation analysis revealed that neither plasma GFAP nor plasma NfL levels had a strong relationship with serum CK values ( Supplementary Figure S3 ). Given the growing evidence of CNS involvement in IOPD, surveillance strategies should extend beyond muscle-based biomarkers to include neurologic biomarkers like GFAP and NfL, along with brain MRI starting around age 5 years, when sedation is generally not required. Future studies with expanded cohorts and longitudinal designs will be essential to validate this framework, clarify the influence of CRIM status on biomarker trajectories, and establish the role of GFAP and NfL in guiding clinical care. It is important to consider the inherent limitations of our study. First, the sample size of patients with IOPD was relatively small, which is expected in rare disease research but may impact generalisability. Due to the small cohort, we evaluated biomarker performance using ROC curves on the entire sample rather than splitting into training and validation sets; as a result, the reported AUC values should be interpreted as indicative of potential performance rather than definitive estimates of generalisable accuracy. Additionally, multiple biomarker values per subject were treated as independent data points. While this maximised the use of available data from this rare disease cohort, it may overestimate significance and favour participants for which more biomarker levels were available. We addressed this by summarising values by patient, however, future studies should employ a prospective design that allows for mixed effect models in order to confirm the predictive capacity of plasma GFAP for specific outcome measures, like WMHI severity. Second, while GFAP correlated with white matter burden on brain MRI, the MFS assesses only white matter and does not capture grey matter changes—potentially explaining elevated GFAP levels even in patients with mild WMHI. Future studies should incorporate neuroimaging methods to assess grey matter and spinal cord involvement, both of which may contribute to GFAP elevations in IOPD. Additionally, GFAP and NfL were measured using research-grade assays that require further standardisation before clinical translation. Third, there were also important age-related considerations that impact the interpretation of our findings. Our LOPD cohort comprised of primarily younger patients which could have limited the generalisability of findings to adults or those with more advanced disease. The IOPD subgroup with severe neurologic involvement had fewer late-teen samples due to earlier mortality and shorter follow-up, and therefore, the age distribution differed from the attenuated subgroup. This imbalance may introduce age-related bias in group comparisons, though we attempted to mitigate this by age-matching controls and by analysing longitudinal trends within each subgroup. NfL levels are physiologically elevated in infancy and decline with age; the inclusion of younger controls likely contributed to higher median NfL values and overlap with patient samples. Because CNS involvement in IOPD is progressive, group-level comparisons that aggregate longitudinal values may be influenced by differences in age and disease stage at the time of sampling, potentially masking trends despite our efforts to age-match controls. However, control samples were cross-sectional, collected during evaluations for non-neurologic indications, and while none had documented CNS disease, undiagnosed or subclinical pathology cannot be fully excluded. In addition, GFAP and NfL were measured using research-grade assays that require further standardisation before clinical translation. Lastly, our preclinical model lacked paired plasma GFAP and NfL measurements, limiting direct comparison between blood biomarkers and CNS histopathology. Conclusion This study identifies plasma GFAP as a sensitive and specific blood-based biomarker of CNS involvement in IOPD. We observed a positive correlation of plasma GFAP levels with WMHI detectable on MRI, as well as elevations in IOPD patients with attenuated neurologic involvement which supports its utility in detecting underlying astrogliosis and subclinical disease. Notably, plasma GFAP levels were not elevated in LOPD, suggesting potential differences in disease pathophysiology between infantile- and late-onset forms of PD. Given its CNS specificity and non-invasive nature, GFAP appears to be a sensitive biomarker of CNS involvement of IOPD and may detect neurological changes earlier and more reliably than NfL; however, longitudinal studies are needed to confirm its temporal dynamics.
